A '''colliding beam machine''' collide [[quantum particle]]s at high-speeds.

== Mechanism ==


[[File:Cornell_electron_storage_ring.jpg|thumbnail|The Cornell Electron Storage Ring accelerates electrons and positrons to 4.5–6 GeV via a linear accelerator and a synchrotron, hold them in the outer storage ring at that energy, then collide them in a particle detector]]
Most colliding beam machines accelerate particles via [[particle accelerator]]s to create two counter-rotating beams of '''collision candidate particles''', then focus them onto one another at the center of a [[particle detector]] at the desired moment.<ref>{{#cite:Q2531}}</ref>

== Capacity ==

The [[quantum particle interaction#Centre-of-mass_energy|centre-of-mass energy]] of the collisions produced in a colliding beam machine $W$ is directly proportional to the beam energy $E_{beam}$.

In general,

$$
W\approx \frac{E_{beam}}{2}
$$

<ref>{{#cite:Q2531}}</ref>

<blockquote>
Particles must be accelerated to higher speeds to produce higher beam energies, which requires larger [[particle accelerator]]s. Modern colliding beam machines can be quite large: e.g., the [[Large Hadron Collider (LHC)]], capable of producing beam energies in excess of $6\mathrm{TeV}$ and currently the largest in the world, is 27-kilometers long. In the 1940s, Italian-American physicist [[Person:Enrico Fermi|Enrico Fermi]] even envisioned a colliding beam machine encircling the earth!
</blockquote>

== Measurement ==

Colliding beam machines include a [[particle detector]] to measure the momentum, energy, and mass of the particles produced by the collision of the beams.

As energy is a [[conserved property]] over collision between quantum particles, the total energy of the product particles is equal to the [[colliding beam machine#Capacity|centre-of-mass energy]] of the collision:

$$
E_{total}=W
$$

In practice, however, the [[particle detector#Energy|total energy of all particles detected in the particle detector]]

$$
E_{\text{total detected}} \lt W
$$

as some particles (e.g., [[neutrino]]s), are difficult to detect.

<ref>{{#cite:Q2531}}</ref>
